key_facts: **Cutaneous small-vessel (leukocytoclastic) vasculitis** presents as **palpable purpura** on the lower legs, often in crops.
Causes: drugs, infection (strep, hepatitis B/C), autoimmune disease, malignancy; up to half idiopathic.
Look for systemic disease: urine dipstick and BP, FBC, U&E, LFT, CRP, ANA, ANCA, complement, hepatitis serology, cryoglobulins.
Biopsy an early lesion (<48 h) for histology and direct IF.
Stop culprit drug, rest, elevation, compression; refer if systemic or recurrent.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: **Leukocytoclastic vasculitis (LCV)** is the histological term for neutrophil-rich small-vessel vasculitis of dermal post-capillary venules. Clinically, when it is **single-organ**, it is called **cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis (CSVV)**, **hypersensitivity vasculitis** or cutaneous leukocytoclastic angiitis (CHCC). [Case 3](condition:cutaneous-vasculitis-approach) is **drug-induced LCV after an NSAID**.

ul: **"Purpura is always low platelets"**: palpable purpura with normal platelets suggests vasculitis.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: Immune complexes trigger **neutrophils to destroy small vessels**.

mech.t: A drug, infection or autoantigen forms immune complexes.
Complexes lodge in post-capillary venules, especially in dependent legs.
Complement attracts neutrophils that fragment (leukocytoclasis) and damage vessels.
mech.caption: Immune complexes and fragmenting neutrophils damage the vessel wall; red cells leak out.

mech.t: Red cells leak, causing raised purpura that does not blanch.

blocks: Immune complexes (drug–antibody) form and deposit in venules, activating complement and attracting neutrophils.

ul: Drug-induced LCV usually starts **7–21 days** after a new drug (sooner on re-exposure; this case says "a few days").

**Why the legs?**: **gravity/hydrostatic pressure** and **venous stasis** in dependent limbs → slower flow and turbulence in post-capillary venules; so immune complexes deposit more readily; plus cooler peripheral temperature; and tight footwear/socks — the same reason it appears on the buttocks/back in people lying in bed; That is why **bed rest, elevation and support hosiery** help

histo: Fibrinoid necrosis of small vessels, neutrophils with nuclear dust, red cell extravasation.

sections.title: Clinical features
blocks: **Symmetrical, non-blanching, palpable purpuric papules and macules (1–3 mm), some coalescing**, on the **lower legs/ankles/dorsal feet**, appearing in crops; ± haemorrhagic vesicles, pustules, small necrotic centres or shallow ulcers; ± mild oedema. Burning/itch. Well otherwise.

ul: **3e — the single bedside test: urinalysis** (dipstick for **blood and protein**). It tells you whether the kidneys are involved (systemic vasculitis/IgA nephritis), which changes urgency and management. Measure BP at the same visit.

**3f — other investigations:** FBC (platelet count — exclude thrombocytopenic purpura; eosinophilia), U&E/eGFR, LFT, CRP/ESR, clotting; **urine ACR/PCR** and microscopy; **ANA, ANCA, C3/C4, RF, cryoglobulins**; **hepatitis B/C, HIV**, ASO/throat swab; **SPEP**/immunofixation; **IgA**; blood cultures if febrile; faecal occult blood if abdominal pain; CXR if respiratory symptoms; **skin biopsy for H&E (LCV) + DIF** (IgA deposition → IgA vasculitis even in adults, with a higher nephritis risk)

sections.title: Differential diagnoses
blocks: IgA vasculitis (HSP — adults, abdominal pain, arthritis, haematuria), urticarial vasculitis, cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis (HCV), ANCA vasculitis (MPA/GPA — renal/lung), vasculitis secondary to CTD (SLE, RA, Sjögren's), septic vasculitis/emboli (endocarditis, meningococcaemia, gonococcaemia), thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP, drug-induced — **NSAIDs rarely cause thrombocytopenia too**), pigmented purpuric dermatosis, stasis/capillaritis, **exercise-induced vasculitis** ("golfer's vasculitis" — after long walks in heat), scurvy, Waldenström hypergammaglobulinaemic purpura.

sections.title: Management

ol: **Stop the NSAID.** Record "NSAID (name) — cutaneous vasculitis" and **Yellow Card**. Advise against OTC NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin in analgesic doses) until specialist advice clarifies cross-reactivity.

**Back pain analgesia without NSAIDs (NICE NG59):** exercise/physiotherapy, heat, and — if needed — a short course of a **weak opioid ± paracetamol** (paracetamol alone is not recommended for low back pain in NG59, but may be used as an adjunct). Avoid gabapentinoids for non-specific back pain.

**General measures:** rest, **leg elevation**, **graduated compression hosiery** (check ABPI/pulses if arterial disease is possible), emollient, potent TCS on symptomatic lesions, antihistamine for itch. Expect resolution in **2–4 weeks**, sometimes with residual pigmentation.

**Ulcerating/necrotic or persistent (>4 weeks) disease:** specialist — **short oral prednisolone course** (e.g. 0.5 mg/kg tapering over 2–4 weeks), **dapsone** (course teaching; 50–100 mg/day after G6PD check; FBC/LFT/methaemoglobin monitoring), **colchicine** 500 micrograms once–twice daily; immunosuppressants for chronic disease.
**Monitoring:** clinical (old lesions healing, new crops) + **ESR/CRP**; repeat **urinalysis and BP** at each review (e.g. weekly while active).

blocks: Within IP scope: stop the NSAID, alternative analgesia, urinalysis/bloods, compression and topical care, Yellow Card, and referral. Systemic steroids/dapsone are usually specialist-advised.

refer.t: Haematuria, proteinuria or rising creatinine: same-day renal advice.
Necrosis, ulceration or purpura above the waist: consider systemic vasculitis and refer urgently.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Haematuria, proteinuria or rising creatinine: same-day renal advice.
Necrosis, ulceration or purpura above the waist: consider systemic vasculitis and refer urgently.

blocks: Haematuria/proteinuria, raised creatinine, hypertension, systemic symptoms, abdominal pain/GI bleed, haemoptysis, neuropathy, necrosis/ulceration, persistence >4 weeks, recurrence, or positive ANCA/cryoglobulins → urgent specialist (rheumatology/renal/dermatology). Fever + purpura + unwell → same day.

ul: Single episodes settle in weeks; chronic forms recur.

pearls: "**Drug, legs, palpable purpura, well patient → stop the drug, dip the urine, elevate.**"
Warn that **new crops can appear for 1–2 weeks** after stopping the drug.

quiz.q: When should you think of Cutaneous small-vessel (leukocytoclastic) vasculitis?
quiz.a: Symmetrical palpable purpura, sometimes with blisters or small ulcers, on the shins and ankles after a new drug or infection.
Immune complexes lodge in small skin vessels, recruit neutrophils and break down (leukocytoclasis).

quiz.q: What is the backbone of care?
quiz.a: Stop the trigger; rest, elevation and compression if no arterial disease; analgesia (not the culprit NSAID); dipstick and bloods; refer if systemic or persistent.
Kidney involvement; IgA vasculitis in children; vasculitis that is part of lupus, ANCA disease or cryoglobulinaemia.

quiz.q: Name a red flag that needs escalation.
quiz.a: Haematuria, proteinuria or rising creatinine: same-day renal advice.
